newsitem.title: GERMANY: German labour relations hit by metal dispute.
newsitem.headline: German labour relations hit by metal dispute.

text.p: Negotiations over a bitter pay dispute in the German metal industry collapsed on Wednesday, raising the prospect of more mass protests by metal workers and a wider deterioration of Germany's once-cosy labour relations.

The break-down of talks also underlines the challenge facing Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in cutting the country's near-record jobless levels while helping industry to secure the labour cost reductions its says are necessary for survival.

IG Metall, Germany's largest union, and the Gesamtmetall engineering employers federation said early on Wednesday that crisis talks on plans by employers to reduce worker benefits within the 1997 wage round had failed.

Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe told a news briefing that the trade union had not budged in its resistance to a new government law allowing companies to cut sick pay allowances from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
"IG Metall sees full sick pay allowances as a sacred cow," Stumpfe said, adding that the union had rejected suggestions of a compromise somewhere between 80-100 percent of salary.
Companies in the sector, including industrial giant Daimler Benz AG, had earlier this month attempted to implement the new law immediately.
But those companies were later forced to postpone the cuts after a protest day that involved more than 100,000 workers and cost Daimler alone some 80 million marks ($50 million).
Daimler said on Wednesday that it was sticking with its promise not to implement the sick pay cuts until a "contractual clarification" with workers on the issue had been reached.
IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel said nonetheless that a further round of protests would now go ahead as planned on Thursday. "It will be a big day," he warned.

Zwickel was the centre figure earlier this year of the so-called "Alliance for Jobs", a failed attempt to revive Germany's tradition of seeking consensus between workers and employers on how industry should be run.

Employment in the metal and engineering sector has fallen since 1991 by around one million jobs to 3.5 million as a result of recession and foreign competition -- a situation employers say has been exacerbated by high labour costs.

But IG Metall argues that employers should now implement measures to protect existing jobs in the sector and has said it would accept a 1997 wage increase in line with inflation if such agreements could be obtained.
Employers for their part would only accept such a rise in wages if it were offset by reductions in other labour costs such as holiday pay and generous Christmas bonuses.
Talks on the 1997 wage round are now likely to be put off until existing wage contracts run out at the end of the year unless further crisis meetings are called.

But Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe said that the sick pay issue and other negotiations on worker conditions would now likely have to be handled by individual companies rather than on a collective level as has been traditionally the case.
Such a weakening of Germany's collective bargaining process is a new setback for the Bonn government in its attempts to juggle the interests of employers with workers.
Earlier this week Kohl was forced into an embarassing admission that a previously-stated goal of halving the country's four million jobless total by the year 2000 could be optimistic.
